rates.what: one token drips into the bucket on each beat while there is room

events.what: request A is admitted and takes a token
burst request C is admitted; the bucket is empty
a drop lands mid-burst as a token
burst request D takes the fresh token at once; the bucket is empty again
burst request E finds no token and is refused with a 429
the next drop lands as a token
one beat later another drop lands
request F is admitted with a refilled token
another drop lands as the view pulls back

moments.title: Open the limiter
moments.change: Small request-rate-limiter glyph → full-size bucket with three tokens at rest; the user chip docks at its left rim; the inlet drop appears, still

moments.title: One request, one token
moments.change: 3 tokens → 2; request A passes through to the API carrying its token; the drop starts to swell

moments.title: A burst outruns the drip
moments.change: 2 tokens → 1 → 0 → 1 (drop lands) → 0; the level empties; the drop resets and starts swelling again

moments.title: Refused
moments.change: E approaches → stops at the empty rim → recoils back along its route with a 429; the bucket stays at 0

moments.title: Hold on the refill
moments.change: 0 tokens → 1 → 2 in two landings one beat apart; the level rises with each

moments.title: Name the rate
moments.change: 2 tokens → 1; request F passes to the API

moments.title: Every bucket, in Redis
moments.change: One large bucket → one of many in the Redis store; ours goes from 1 token to 2

question: How is a per-user limit actually enforced?
takeaway: Each request spends one token from its user's bucket. A burst spends tokens faster than the drip returns them, so the bucket empties and the next request is refused; the drip keeps refilling at a steady rate. Every user's bucket lives centrally, in Redis.
